utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Wednesday, June 11, 2008, and I greet the representatives of the OTP, our witness, as well as Mr. Seselj and everyone helping us. I have an oral decision to deliver. It requires private session. The witness is here, and I don't have a problem with this, because no names are mentioned. There's only a number that is mentioned. So let's move to private session, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you can put your headset back on. Thank you for your patience. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor. So far, you've used up 21 minutes. You have one hour and thirty-nine minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Koblar, you described during the examination-in-chief a locality at Golo Brdo and these bunkers where you were together with your group. You described heavy artillery fire at these bunkers, and then you made statements to the contrary in several of your statements, as a matter of fact. In the statement that you gave to the OTP in 2004, you say that these bunkers were very well built, and in other statements you say that these bunkers were poorly built. What is the truth, then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes, yes, thank you, now I can see. I'm waiting for the translation to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are they interpreting into Bosnian for you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated clearly, in both statements to the OTP and in the statement that I assume you do have, that these were exceptionally strong bunkers, which means that this artillery fire that went on for two hours, at least, before the attack of the police of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Chetnik unit of Vojislav Seselj, or, rather, Brne Gavrilovic, they started crumbling these bunkers. I never said that they were poorly built. I just stated that these bunkers -- or, rather, that from these bunkers, we could not see the attackers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Were these fortified or unfortified bunkers?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 0021-5347 on the screen? That is the statement that Mr. Koblar gave on the 19th of February, 1994, on the official premises of the Military Security Service of the 101st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Registrar is telling me that the text is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judges, for the OTP, it is a 15-minute job to load it up in e-court, and this is a major omission on their part; not to have done that, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On page 2 of that document, of that statement of yours, it says: "In view of the fact that the bunkers had not been fortified, we all sought shelter in one bunker, rather, five or six of us." So you keep repeating that they were fortified, the bunkers were, and that is what you said to the OTP investigators in 2004, and ten years before that you say that the bunkers had not been fortified. How come there is this contradiction?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no contradiction whatsoever. In the statement that I made, my unit after escaping from the camp, I said that these were Serb military positions at Golo Brdo and that the bunkers were exceptionally fortified. As for the context that you are referring to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where does it say in your statement that these were Serb military positions? In the statement that you gave in 1994 to the Military Security Service of the 101st Brigade, you made no reference to that. Do you remember that statement of yours? Let the OTP show you that statement. I request and demand that the OTP be instructed to have this statement handed over to the witness, and it's not my fault that e-court is not functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: For the record, I read that Mr. Seselj said that it was a major omission on the OTP, on their part, not to have done that, regarding to the up-load the statement into e-court. I want to specify that it is not the obligation of the OTP to put a statement in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ferrara. I had noted that myself. But now we have the text on the ELMO, so, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, they insisted that I appoint a person who would be trained to use e-court systems on my behalf, and they even made that offer to me, to train to be able to use e-court. And now all of a sudden it is not the obligation of the OTP to upload this. Now, who is saying the truth here? You can conclude that for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In this statement of yours that has been placed before you, you can see that there is no reference to Serb bunkers whatsoever, and on page 22468, line 8, on the second page -- could you please place the second page on the ELMO -- it says that the bunkers were unfortified and that, therefore, you all sought shelter in one bunker, or, rather, five or six of you did. Do you have this in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come I don't? Oh, yes, I see it now, yes, line 8. See, it's appeared: "Since the bunkers were not fortified, we all sought shelter that one bunker." So you said they were not fortified, right, and now you're saying they were well fortified, the bunkers?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accused, have you read the statement in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're not supposed to put questions to me. I am putting questions to you. You explain to me why, in 1994, 14 years ago, you said that the bunkers were unfortified, and four years ago that they were fortified, and today you repeat that they were fortified. Why? And you cannot address me as "accused." Let me make that abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... sir, answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortified bunkers, from the point of view of the BiH Army, mean that we could not defend Golo Brdo from those bunkers in any situation. After two or three hours - I don't know how long this went on -- I am going to speak at this pace in order to give the interpreters time to interpret. The shelling from Lukavica and from the surrounding hills where the Serb artillery was, led to the fact that these bunkers had to crumble, so that is the context. Now, you have been trying to find another context, but this is the context in which this statement was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You invented something else now, that the shelling went on for two or three hours, whereas in this statement from 1994, you say that shells were falling for 40 minutes and that you were in hiding that long, and that you could not go to different bunkers. And when there was a lull in the shelling, then "we went to different bunkers." Look at this statement of yours. That's what it says. When was it that you were fabricating or inventing things, then or now? Did you all seek shelter in one bunker?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven of us. That is clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it stated that you remained in hiding for 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Question from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I think this kind of language is not appropriate to a cross-examination, saying that the witness is inventing something or fabricating something. I ask the Trial Chamber to warn the accused to use appropriate language for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if there's a contradiction, ask him why there is a contradiction. You're not here to draw the conclusion that he invented this. If you find that there are contradictions, confront him with these contradictions, and it will be up to the Trial Chamber to draw the conclusions. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what you are allowing here is the witness putting questions to me and that he is addressing me in an inappropriate manner, and I have to intervene personally to defend myself from that. He's supposed to answer questions, and nothing more than that. He's not here to put questions to me. I am asking him why it says in his statement that the shelling went on for 40 minutes and now he says that it went on for two or three hours. Everything that I am doing now has an interior logic of its own which is still hidden to you, but it will not remain hidden for very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber asked -- told the witness twice that he was supposed to answer, so now you are saying things that are not exact at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, furthermore, you should tell the witness the following: "You made two statements, one saying that the shelling lasted for 40 minutes, and the other one, that the shelling lasted for two to three hours," and then you should tell him, "Explain and tell us why there is such a difference." And then the witness will explain or answer, rather than saying immediately that he's making up things or fabricating all this. Maybe he's got a reason to explain why there's this difference. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where were the shooting points facing?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Hrasnica, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the statement that you made on the 19th of February, 1994, the statement that you made to the same service, but this is a longer statement, one that is 34 pages long, why did you state that these bunkers did not have any loopholes at all; why?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the entrances to these bunkers, and these bunkers and these loopholes, were actually made of rocks facing Sarajevo. We could not use that, except for one MRUD, and you know what that is, and that could not have been used at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is a mine? What is this MRUD?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a Claymore mine. You know that full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the statement that you made on that day, but on many more pages, on page 600653168 is the number, you stated that these bunkers had not been adapted to firing at all and that they do not have loopholes for shooting. And now you say that there were loopholes, but that they were facing in another direction. Now, what is the truth?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am repeating once again --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, he cannot address me this way. He has to answer questions. He cannot say, "Accused, I am repeating to you once again."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, answer the question put to you by the accused. He's asking you about the bunkers, to know whether there were those loopholes or not, whether they were facing Sarajevo or not. I'm a bit lost at the moment. I have no idea where the accused wants to take us, but he obviously has his own logic. You were there, you were in the bunker, so you're the best one to tell us exactly what the bunker was like. So just tell us quietly whether there were loopholes or not. You don't have to worry about anything. Just answer the questions. Mr. Seselj, you may resume, and try to elicit the evidence that you want to elicit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the statement that this witness made on that same day in 1994, it says, and we have it before us on the screens, it's towards the end of the second paragraph: "I have to note here that while touring the positions that we had arrived at, I established that the bunkers were not adapted for a situation of firing. They do not have loopholes or gun-holes, and there was no shelter in front of them in order to be able to fire securely. It is my assessment that these bunkers were only used for the accommodation of people and for their rest." That is what the witness said in 1994, and now the witness is saying something completely different. Now he is saying that these were old Serb bunkers that were facing in the opposite direction, that used to be made by Serbs and used against the Muslims, and that's why their gun-holes faced the other positions. So that's the contradiction involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will try to explain this as briefly as possible. Since we, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in respect of this important feature above Sarajevo, Golo Brdo, we arrived there to guard that feature, there is no contradiction involved, because this statement was given from my very own point of view as a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. From those positions, from those gun-holes, none of us could defend ourselves. Why would we be defending ourselves from the direction of Igman, Bjelasnica, or Hrasnica, instead of defending ourselves from the direction of Ilidza, Blazuj and Hadzici? There is no contradiction involved, because I think that Mr. -- now I'm going to say "Seselj," is better acquainted with total national defence, and to suggest questions like this to the Court is actually just an attempt to suggest one's own views, because it was well known who was the aggressor at the time and the attacker, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, who was defending themselves, whereas I and my 24 colleagues at Golo Brdo could not defend ourselves from these bunkers. And I said all of this to your man, who is a greater man than you are, Branislav Gavrilovic, because he proved himself a man during the course of the war, at least at the time that I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, Judges, that you are quietly listening to the witness lecture you. Maybe you even learned that lesson, but still you should not allow the witness to act in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you might not like the witness's answer. As far as I'm concerned, his answer is perfectly logical. This position in Golo Brdo was above Sarajevo. He realised, when he was there, that from his position, he could not defend himself from these bunkers. He is providing a technical explanation for this, and he is saying that it was important to make a distinction of who was the enemy of whom. You might not be happy with his answer, and you put other questions to him to question what he's saying. And this is why you jump out of your skin, because you are saying that he has said this already to Gavrilovic. So he's consistent in what he's saying. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't doubt that you would find this very consistent, because you're on the opposite side, and what is not consistent to me, by the logic of things, has to be consistent to you. This is completely logical to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not on the opposite side. We have a witness here who is providing his account of the story. He might be telling the truth, he might be lying, but at first hand he has taken the solemn declaration and we assume that what he is saying is truthful. You may disagree entirely with what he's saying, and you are making his life difficult by putting your questions to him. That is why these proceedings unfold in this manner in an adversarial system in this courtroom. It is not because a witness does not provide answers in line with what you expect from him that you need to accuse the witness of something. You might be right, he might be right. He might be wrong, you might be wrong. We will see at the end of this trial. For the time being, he's providing us with his version of the facts, which is logical. And the way he talks about it, it's for you to demonstrate that this illogical. This is what you did yesterday when you discussed the issue of the tunnel under the airport. This was very interesting, and your questions were very interesting. I found them extremely relevant, and it did shed some light on some of the issues. I didn't say so yesterday, I didn't say that your questions were out of context. Today, I'm saying the same thing. Your questions are extremely interesting. The witness is answering in a different manner to what you expect from him, and you can say to him, "I disagree with you," and move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see you are encouraging the witness in the insolence he already displayed. Well, then, you explain to me, Mr. President, why he said in 1994 that the bunkers had no gun-holes at all and now he says they had gun-holes but they were facing the opposite way. And that they were not fortified bunkers but bunkers to accommodate personnel, and now he says they are fortified. Why isn't it indicated in the statement to Bosnian authorities that those used to be Serb bunkers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you will never manage to confuse the Bench, however talented you are. Let me pick up the question again, and you will see that what you are trying to establish comes up against what the witness is saying. Witness, if I have understood you correctly, there is a hill above Sarajevo. Answer by saying "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Golo Brdo, where I was arrested, captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On this hill, there are some bunkers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nine bunkers. Now, over time, these bunkers had been placed there for what reason; to defend who against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those bunkers were built by the Army of Republika Srpska. I will give the interpreters a breather. Until the day I was captured, that was the 17th of July, they changed hands more than once. I hope you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Nine bunkers were built by the Republika Srpska in order to defend themselves against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whom they were supposed to be defending themselves from. Those bunkers were built in order to attack Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Republika Srpska has built nine bunkers in order to attack Sarajevo. The gun-holes were in which direction, in the direction of Sarajevo or on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Facing Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the gun-holes pointed in the direction of Sarajevo? In other words, if you were to place artillery pieces or guns, these would shoot in the direction of Sarajevo. When you reached the bunkers, well, the bunkers were still there, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both the bunkers and the gun-holes faced Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, in the statement given to Muslim authorities, you said the bunkers had no gun-holes?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my statement to the Military Security Service of my unit, the 101st Brigade, not to Muslim authorities. In that statement, I'm saying this again, it is clearly stated -- I don't remember how many pages there are in that statement -- why I was giving that statement. And you're saying this is a contradiction, but it all depends on your point of view. We were supposed to defend Golo Brdo, not to shoot at Sarajevo from Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, in the statement from 1994, did you say that those bunkers had no gun-holes?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no gun-holes in case of attack by the Serb Army or Chetnik units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here they had no gun-holes whatsoever and they were not adapted to cases of gunfire, and the space around them had no cover for protection. You said in your opinion, they were there only to accommodate personnel in times of rest. If they were made for rest and to accommodate personnel, they are not facing any side in particular. And let me tell you, Judges, that a bunker is a defensive structure, not an offensive structure. It cannot be built to attack something or someone. A bunker is not a tank to roll on caterpillars.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. From that feature, Golo Brdo, there was never any artillery fire. That hill, Golo Brdo, was an elevation overlooking Ilidza from which one could see Lukavica, the airport, all of Sarajevo, the neighbourhood of Ilidza. The only thing that was not visible was Blazuj and Hadzici. Blazuj and Hadzici, though, were under the control of the Serb Army. Therefore, that hill, Golo Brdo, was used by the Army of Republika Srpska to control the road of Mount Igman that was used to bring humanitarian aid into Sarajevo, to control the Sarajevo Airport --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I understand what you are saying. Mr. Seselj doesn't want understand what you are saying. You're saying that if there were an attack from Blazuj or Hadzici -- I apologise for my pronunciation -- which were under Serb control, you could not defend yourselves because there were no gun-holes pointing in that direction, since they faced the Sarajevo Airport and the rest of the area. This is what I have understood. Am I right in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am in awe, Mr. President, at your understanding. I am too dumb to understand why it's written here that those were not combat bunkers at all, that they had no gun-holes, they were only bunkers used exclusively as shelter. It's not clear to me because I'm too dumb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Second question: Since we've established I'm dumb, it's easier now to proceed. You said that after this artillery attack, you returned each to your own bunker. You were not alone in one bunker, were you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was it, then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the first bunker -- you can read that in the statement -- in the first bunker there were three men, in the second bunker two, but at the moment of the artillery attack, we were seven. So in that bunker in which I was, together with Hilmija Numic, and I'll be waiting for the interpreters, after the beginning of the artillery attack we were in the second bunker which is on top of Golo Brdo. And when there occurred a lull and the bunkers crumbled in, we caved in, we transferred to the third bunker which is at the very end of Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one point I'd like you to clarify for the Bench. The nine bunkers that were built by the Republika Srpska, according to what I've understood, but maybe I have misunderstood, these bunkers were designed to help -- were designed to be able to shoot at Sarajevo and the airport, and the Serbs could shoot from there. That was the initial purpose of this bunker, and that's why there were gun-holes on it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, and I would appreciate it if you could allow me to indicate on the monitor what it looks like, approximately, the purpose of that Golo Brdo was to control the airport, the Igman road, and to control the arrival of humanitarian aid into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To control, if need be, by shooting at those people that got into the way of the control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. And Richard Holbrooke wrote in his book, and "The War," I believe, is the title, said that the first American officers to get killed were killed by fire from Golo Brdo on the Igman road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you understood, Mr. President, that it was not possible to shoot from Golo Brdo at Sarajevo, because there's no such weapon. You could possibly use a Howitzer of 203 millimetres, but that sort of thing does not fit into the bunker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said there was any heavy artillery on Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are interfering with my dialogue with the Judges, and that is not allowed either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, to avoid wasting any time, the witness is telling us that Richard Holbrooke, in his book, explained that American officers were killed and shot at from Golo Brdo. I don't know anything about this. The witness is saying this. You probably know more about this than I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not interested in that, Judge. I'm not interested in how American officers died. I wish many more had died. They got killed because they strayed into a minefield and their vehicle ended up in an abyss. They did not get killed by fire from Serbian positions. It doesn't matter how they got killed. I only wish more of them had got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. There might be a mistake in the translation into French. I have the feeling that you are saying that not enough people were killed, more should have been killed. This is what I understood, but maybe you didn't say this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I wish we were fortunate enough to see more of them get killed, because the greater American losses, the less repression there would be on the rest of the world. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said this fire lasted for half an hour, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: It is really inappropriate, this kind of conduct by the accused. It's not a cross-examination, it's not a question. I don't know what it is. It is a political speech or something else, but I don't think it is something that should happen in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the cross-examination -- during cross-examination, you should put questions to the witness to call into question what he has said when he answered the questions of the Prosecution. All the rest is inappropriate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In this 1994 statement, you said that the shelling lasted for half an hour and that the shooting was directed at the bunker in which you were, and then the shooting stopped. When the shooting stopped, you went outside the bunker, you left the bunker. And then a little further on, you go on to say that you went to your own bunker, taking up a shirt and a leather jacket, because nearby you could hear explosions. And then you go on to say that they were explosions caused by hand grenades. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it says in that statement, because it was given several days after I fled from the camp, but once again you're trying to put words into my mouth. Things that I uttered, but you're trying to interpret them and put them in your own way, and you can't do that. I'm here to testify about what I lived through, what I saw.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why don't you intervene, Mr. President? Why doesn't he answer my questions? Were hand grenades thrown or not, were there hand grenades explosions or not? This is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is -- the question is: "Were hand grenades used, yes or no?" You answer by saying "yes" or "no," even if the accused is trying to make you change what you said during your first statements. Either you stand by what you said in your statements or you change your view. You can say "yes," "no," "I disagree." Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the answer to my question, which was: After the shelling, were there explosions, hand grenade explosions?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what a hand grenade sounds like when it explodes or a [indiscernible] or whatever, but the explosions were less strong than the previous ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were in the bunker and you heard these explosions close by; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around -- at Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not at Golo Brdo, but in the vicinity. That's what you said in your statement; isn't that right ? It says: "In my immediate vicinity, explosions could be heard, and I didn't know what had caused them. It was only later on that I established that they were hand grenades exploding." That's your 1994 statement. Now, the statement that you gave to The Hague investigators in 2004, on page 4 of that statement it says: "My rifle was next to me, and I stayed in the bunker for about ten minutes, long enough to button up my shirt and put on my leather jacket. My rifle was next to me, and I could hear explosions at that time which had not come from artillery pieces but from hand grenades or hand-held launchers."

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So your bunkers were shot at either by hand-held launchers, which were popularly known as "Zoljas," those were hand-held rocket-launchers, right, or hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is in the army, but it could be Zoljas, hand-held rocket-launchers, or it can be what we called a Tromblon, a rifle-launch grenade, or rifle-propelled grenade, but I'm not a specialist in weapons and military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Whether it was a rifle-propelled grenade or a hand grenade or a hand-held launcher, because you don't use the word Tromblon or rifle-propelled grenade anywhere, but they were -- that was firing in the vicinity of your bunker, wasn't it ?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can I explain to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've answered. You said "yes." So hand pieces were used to target your bunker? There wasn't any shooting from rifles; you didn't hear anything like that, did you? Did you hear a single bullet being fired from a rifle?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All you heard were hand grenades; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the Serb soldiers approached your bunker and started throwing hand grenades at it, or they targeted it from a distance of 200 metres, at most, with hand-held rocket-launchers, so when you use a rifle-propelled grenade, that would be firing at a distance of 200 metres, 300 at the outside limit. That's when you fire close up, close to.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you going to ask me a question or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I am making an observation, and I expect you to give a yes-or-no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please answer the questions accurately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you repeat the question, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I won't, because this kind of insolence I'm not going to tolerate. The Trial Chamber can tolerate you, but I won't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can the Trial Chamber then ask the question again, repeat the question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: The witness is asking to repeat the question. I don't see any kind of insolence, also because I don't see the question, also. And if you can read the transcript, I don't see a question; I see like a kind of a statement without any question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I didn't quite understand the question, so put the question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not going to repeat the question and ask it again, because you're just wasting my time. This whole machinery is put in place to waste my time. I'm going to move on. I'm not interested in what the witness is going to answer, what answer he's going to give. It's quite clear to me and it's quite clear to the public, and that is enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, shooting at your bunkers had to be -- had to cause certain losses. Hand grenades are being thrown into your bunker right from nearby, or rifle-held grenades or hand-held rocket-launchers. How come nobody was killed in your immediate vicinity from the effects of all that shooting? Tell me that, then.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are going to come back now to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. Answer the present one.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer that question as well. How --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't allow the witness to do this. Let him answer how come there were no losses from this direct fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question put by Mr. Seselj is an interesting one. When Mr. Seselj puts good questions, I say so. When he puts bad questions, I say so also. He has asked the following question: How is it that in light of the attack and that there is shooting with Zoljas, rocket-launchers, that you are inside the bunker, there are no victims on your side? That's the question he's put to you. I could have put that question to you also, because this is a question of a technical nature. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That question has been answered already. That question has already been put by the gentleman concerning positions of the bunkers. The answer to the question, why there were no losses, lies precisely in the fact that the bunkers were positioned in such a way that none of us in the BH Army was able to see. I've said that in my previous answer, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I had understood. Given the position of the gun-holes and the attackers, when they arrived and started shooting with their weapons, first of all, their shots could not penetrate the bunker because there were no gun-holes, since they were coming from another direction, which explains why no one was hit, since a bunker is designed to protect even if you shell it with heavy shells. Grenades could not have been thrown inside, since the gun-holes faced the other way. This is what you've just said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. That was the answer to the prior question about this contradiction concerning bunkers on Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Serbian soldiers come from the direction where these gun-holes were, allegedly, although they didn't exist, or from the direction where the entrance to the bunkers is?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb units came at these first two bunkers, where the four of us were, did not come. It was the unit of Branislav Gavrilovic that came from the direction of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Answer my question, please. A Chetnik unit is always a Serb unit, and when that Serb unit arrived, brimming with Chetniks, did it come from the direction of the alleged gun-holes or from the direction where the entrance to the bunkers was located? Answer that.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I don't understand why you identify all Serbs with Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because every honourable Serb is a Chetnik. Answer my question. You didn't come here to learn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question is not to know whether there were Chetniks or whether it was a Serbian unit. This is another problem. Right now, we are looking at a technical problem. You have fighters coming, headed by Gavrilovic. We know that on your side there are no casualties. Mr. Seselj says that since the loopholes are looking at Sarajevo, the entrance must have been on the side of the attackers. This is what he's saying. It might be right, it might be wrong, but he's asking you where the attackers came from. You said exactly that they were coming from a direction that seemed to be on the opposite side of the loopholes, but was there -- on that side were there the entrance doors to the bunker?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no doors, there was just an entrance to the bunker, something that was dug, a little entrance that was dug into the bunker. There were no doors on any of the bunkers. Let the witness answer from which direction the Serb soldiers, the brave heroes, appeared and captured him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really have to make a distinction here. The Army of Republika Srpska came from the direction of Blazuj and Hadzici, whereas the unit of Branislav Gavrilovic, the Chetnik unit, came from the direction of Ilidza; that is, the segment that we were not able to see at all. The Army of Republika Srpska, on the other hand, and the military police of the Army of Republika Srpska came from the direction of Blazuj and Hadzici, another area that could not be covered from bunkers. I want to make that really clear, because Branislav Gavrilovic's unit is one thing, the military police of the Republika Srpska and the Army of Republika Srpska are another thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I think this makes no sense at all, and you keep tolerating it. I'm asking where the Serb soldiers who captured him came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't say it makes no sense and you're tolerating it. The witness is giving up his explanation. He is saying that there are two directions, one coming from Republika Srpska and the military police who left Blazuj, and came from Blazuj, and that's the first unit. And he says there's another unit headed by Gavrilovic, and according to him these are Chetniks, and he says that they come from Ilidza. I fully understand what he is saying. Maybe you're having a hard time understanding what he is saying, but this is exactly what he is saying. If you do not agree with this, tell him that there was only one unit and not two. You may be right. But he is giving us his explanation, and his explanation is perfectly understandable. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am in awe at your perfect understanding. The witness said in the statement there were no gun-holes at all. Here, he said there were gun-holes. I keep persistently asking one and the same question and wasting my own half hour. From which direction did the Serb soldiers come from, the direction where the gun-holes were or the direction where the entrance to the bunker was? And he goes into the tactical situation on the battlefield and the axis of movement of various Serb units. What kind of thing is this? I am asking: Where did the Serb soldiers who captured him come from; from up front, where the gun-holes were, or from the back, where the entrance to the bunker is? It's a simple question, and he keeps avoiding the answer, and I know why he's avoiding the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you. The unit of Branislav Gavrilovic came from the direction of Ilidza, where those already overgrown gun-holes looking at Sarajevo existed, looking also towards Hrasnica and the airport, so they came from the direction from which none of us in the bunker could be seen, because the entrance to the bunker faces the Ilidza road. I don't know how else to explain it. Maybe the Prosecutor will enable me to draw it, what this Golo Brdo looks like. Did you have any occasion to see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I climbed it.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You even went up there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did go up there, and I saw the place where you were defeated, and I publicly commended Branislav Gavrilovic on the brilliant action.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Brne is a ten-times greater man than you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, what is this? The first bunker they came across, Brne's soldiers alone without Brne, because they were led by Zuti, that's the nickname of the soldier who was Brne's deputy, his nickname was Zuti, the first bunker they came across was the one in which three of your fellow combatants were, Zivko Krajisnik, Robert, and Rusmir. Was that the first one?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All three of them, these soldiers killed with hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That's a pure lie on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's true. They killed them with hand grenades, and then you, who were in the second bunker, surrendered, and another three of you, including that Serb, Despotovic, also surrendered. You said here that you recognised the body of Rusmir Hamalukic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. President, to slow these things down, because things are being suggested to me here, things that are lies. I came here to testify about what was true, what happened, not to deal with these lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us what happened with Robert, Rusmir and Krajisnik. You gave us your explanation. Mr. Seselj is entitled to give another explanation. He is entitled to that, and he just gave us his explanation. He said that in the attack on the first bunker, the attack was headed by Zuti. And during this attack headed by Zuti, hand grenades were launched, and according to him, your comrades were killed by these hand grenades. This is what he is telling us, and he is asking questions to you about this. Either say that you agree or you don't agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President, what he is saying, what he is putting to me, but please do not allow us to jump from one subject to another, because he's just trying to impose his own opinion both on me and on you. Please give enough time for what he's saying to be interpreted to you, because I understand him, and then we can go back to the first bunker, the second bunker, and a third bunker. The first and the second bunker was captured by Brne's Chetniks, and a third bunker was captured by the police of Republika Srpska. That's the point, because this is not a bazaar, this is a court of law, and some kind of procedure has to be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in order to maintain respect and decorum in this courtroom, we have repeatedly instructed both parties not to accuse witnesses of lying, and so therefore I would suggest that you abstain from accusing Mr. Seselj from lying as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're entitled to give us your version of what happened. You're under oath, so you must be telling the truth. However, the accused is entitled to give another version of the facts. Even if you don't like it, he is entitled to say that he does not agree with your version, and you must answer his question, all his questions. And in the end, the Bench will decide who was right, whether it was you or him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it's not up to me to judge, but I'd just like you not to allow this tempo to proceed, him to proceed at this rate. I don't know the speed at which the interpreters can interpret and what they're interpreting to you, what you're hearing from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry. Our interpreters can follow. They can follow you when you're talking. The interpreters are interpreting simultaneously. I can even follow Mr. Seselj, even though he's speaking extremely fast. When we lose track of what is said, you know, and when something's missing, we have a little caret on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have the transcript in English in front of your eyes? Well, if you do, you know, you can see that when people speak too fast, interpreters can't follow anymore, and our court reporter, this person at the back of the room, is trying to write down everything we're saying, and if he can't catch what we said, he puts a carat. And then we have to slow down. But otherwise, we don't have to. Mr. Seselj, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you stated that Rusmir Hamalukic's body was -- that a postmortem was conducted on it, and that was in 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said you recognised him because of the red pants he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were red or not, I don't know, but the identification was done in the presence of his mother and wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was DNA analysis done?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need, because the relatives, both his wife and his mother, were there and they recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, how did you manage to come by Rusmir Hamalukic's body?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rusmir Hamalukic's corpse, I think whether it was exchanged or however, I don't really know, but perhaps a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the Serb Army gave up his body, right, handed over his body?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbian army handed over the body of Zivko Krajisnik and this other man, Robert, whatever his surname was; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kahrimanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska handed over their bodies, too, and an autopsy was conducted. Now, when you talked to The Hague investigators, did you tell them this autopsy had taken place, because I can't see that from your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say "autopsy," I said -- not "autopsy," autopsy is one thing. What I said was identification on the basis of -- you're a better lawyer than I am, I assume, or perhaps I'm better than you. I don't know. But, anyway, identification was conducted on the basis of certain elements which the family --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We dealt with identification. You took part in the identification process. Now, when those bodies were handed over, ex officio, an autopsy had to be conducted; that's always done.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't involve me in political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did an autopsy take place? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that and I'm not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Autopsies aren't political, usually. Right, you say you don't know whether an autopsy was conducted. But, Judges, the Prosecutor has not taken the trouble to access the autopsy findings to see whether they were killed by explosion, by a rifle, if they were killed on the spot, or whether any of them had their throats slit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj is addressing an important technical matter. In 1994, a long time after these people passed away, when corpse were exchanged, because unfortunately at the time corpses were exchanged, three corpses were shown to the relatives of Mr. Rusmir Hamalukic, and you're saying that the body [as interpreted] the body. Well, in the past, you know, I've seen a number of -- you say the family recognised the body, and so I've seen a good number of bodies in my own time, and I would like to know what could be recognised in this body. There could have been an autopsy, maybe, but if you only have the skeleton left, well, sometimes if you've got bullet holes, you might determine the impact of the bullets on the bones, but if you only have a skeleton and if the bullet hit no bone, then it's extremely difficult to determine the cause of death. There's a good number of problems here. Then, furthermore, after months or years, the face is changed or is gone. It's very difficult to recognise a body. That's a first problem. Now, according to you, the family recognised it 100 per cent? How were they so sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zivko Krajisnik was recognised -- well, you can check this out through the commission searching for -- state commission searching for missing persons of Amor Masovic, on the basis of which if, because I don't deal in medicine, if it was indeed an autopsy, then it was conducted, and judging by the bones, they could see that some 20 bullets had pierced the body, mostly through the bones. Now, Rusmir Hamalukic's body was identified on the basis of, first and foremost, well, his relatives. That is to say, his wife and mother recognised him, recognised his corpse. And my contribution was only inasmuch as in that mass of bodies that were there, I possibly managed to recognise something which reminded me of Rusmir Hamalukic because Robert Kahrimanovic was identified by his family while I was still in the camp. So that I can't go into medical details. Don't ask me about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this is an important point. You said at least 20 bullets had hit Robert Kahrimanovic and you could see that based on the traces on the bones?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The people who conducted the autopsy did that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about Zivko Krajisnik. I saw Copo kill him before my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what you saw. I'm interested in the results of the autopsy. First of all, you said that you didn't know whether an autopsy had been conducted and that was a political question. Now we see that an autopsy was indeed carried out and that the traces of 20 bullets were found in a body.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, it is scandalous that the Prosecution should bring in a witness testifying about alleged killings, whereas autopsies were carried out on those bodies without the autopsy findings being presented to us, because if the people were killed by hand grenades, offensive hand grenades, they have several thousand metal pieces, many of which must have lodged in the bones, and therefore should be found on the basis of an autopsy. Now the witness says, first of all, he doesn't know whether or not an autopsy was conducted. Then he tries to renege and say that it's a political issue, and then he says, yes, there was an autopsy and that allegedly traces of bullets were shown. Well, I don't know. What is all this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Here we have an eyewitness, and here we have an accused that says that he doesn't want to know what the witness watched but want to know what the witness know about autopsy of somebody. Mr. Koblar is not an expert in forensic medicine, so I don't know -- I don't understand why he's asking a question on autopsy and not on what he watched when he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I thought I understood that when the bodies were brought back, at one point in time you were involved in the identification process. Is it true, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was called to the identification by the State Commission for Exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Apart for Robert Kahrimanovic, who was identified earlier on while I was still in the camp. He was identified by his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you tell us what state the bodies you saw were in? What was left; hair, bones, some flesh, rotten flesh? This is horrible, of course, but what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how can a corpse look a year after death? I think the question should be addressed to Mr. Amor Masovic or someone from the State Commission, somebody that deals with medicine and is better versed in medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... the body of this person a year after his death, what was left? Was it just a skeleton or was there some flesh left? What did the body look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What remained were parts of the uniform, what remained on them. There was something there. But the body, well, it was a skeleton, although there were some other pieces there as well, bodily parts, parts of -- now, let me repeat, I'm not an expert, I'm not an expert in medicine, so I can't really explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you were not alone. There must have been a forensic officer with you or a police officer who was there to make reports, to note that on this body, for example, there are bullet holes, that maybe the femur is fractured, and so forth and so on. Was there a person noting everything down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A forensic pathologist, as far as I remember. Yes, the forensic pathologist, the president of the State Commission, Amor Masovic, his two deputies, the relatives of the people. I can't remember the name now of the pathologist from the Faculty of Medicine. Patogija, I think his surname was, Patogija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So reports must have been drafted, and this report must be somewhere. Maybe Mr. Seselj has it. If the report exists, the conclusions in this report must be there, so to know whether they were killed by a bullet or rather killed by a grenade or something else. The Bench has nothing. You know, that's the difficulty. So, Mr. Seselj, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who killed Robert Kahrimanovic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never saw the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the statement given to The Hague investigators, you said that he was killed by a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska. Somebody who didn't belong to Brne's unit, then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were lying down in a position like this [indicates]. Just imagine yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not interested in your lying-down position. All I'm interested in is on page 6 of your statement to The Hague Tribunal, you said that Robert Kahrimanovic was killed by a soldier of Republika Srpska and four Chetniks jumped up to prevent the killing; right? Four of Brne's soldiers, right, that you call Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: How else can I call them?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, all honourable Serbs are Chetniks. There's no doubt about that. I'm not defending myself from that. But, anyway, four of Brne's soldiers jumped up to prevent the soldier from another unit from killing Robert Kahrimanovic, but he nonetheless killed him because he shot him in the spine with a bullet?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was four of them who jumped up or ten of them who jumped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not important. The important thing is that you stated that he was killed by a soldier of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't you say a moment ago that they were killed by hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm talking about your statements and pointing out the contradictions in them now. How was Rusmir Hamalukic killed, then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say, because I didn't see it happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the statement you gave here to the military security organs, you state that at that moment, one of the Chetniks shot a burst of gunfire and killed Zivko and Rusmir, and that is on page 4 of that shorter statement of yours to the Muslim authorities. May we have it on the overhead projector, please, so that you Judges can see how the witness is lying.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You seem to use the word "lie" every other word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is the first time I've used the word since you've been testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mr. Seselj, just a minute. Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has told you over and over again that you're not supposed to say that a witness is lying. You can say that there are contradictions, but as to drawing the conclusion of lying or not, this is up to the Judges to do so. Right now, the witness is giving up his version of the facts. You might have another one. Give him your version of the facts, and according to his answers we will try and determine where the truth really lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could page 4 from the shorter version of the statement given to the Muslim authorities be put on the overhead projector. The witness has just stated that he didn't see how Rusmir Hamalukic was killed, whereas in the statement he says he did see it. And that is somewhere in the middle of the page, a little above the middle perhaps. Do we have it on our screens now? It hasn't appeared on my yet. Ah, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, he says: "At that moment ..." Do you see where it says that, Mr. Koblar? "At that moment," it's where the arrow is, "one of the Chetniks shot a burst of gunfire and killed Zivko and Rusmir." And now you say that you didn't see when Rusmir Hamalukic was actually killed, so what's the truth of it?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you move down the page so we can see the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that your signature, or perhaps the Prosecution forged it, at the end -- the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to move this. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you understand Serbian? It's at the bottom, the bottom of the page. Is that your signature down there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you signed this statement which you don't recall, and you said in it that one of the Chetniks shot a burst of gunfire and killed Zivko and Rusmir; is that correct? Zivko and Rusmir.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you remind me of the date of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The date is the 19th of February, 1994, in the official premises of the Security Service of the 101st Motor ised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days after I fled from the camp, the minefield, and you want me to remember what I said, what I said exactly at that time? I told The Hague Tribunal, to the OTP, that I saw with my very own eyes who and in what way killed Zivko Krajisnik. And now this statement and this investigation was conducted by Cedic, Sacir, Sacir Cedic, a man who held me in custody and detention, because he asked me to sign some statements because I fled, or rather crossed sides rather than escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we shall not waste time. We have a document here that has been signed by you, and the text is unambiguous. You say they were both killed by a burst of gunfire, which means that you saw them, when you made your statement before the investigators in 1994. This is very clear and very accurate. Now you have come here. You have not said the same thing. This is a problem which the accused has highlighted. When you gave this statement, you were not sure of what you were saying and you said that, or is it that you were very sure and now you're not so sure? This doesn't mean that you're lying. You can be sure of something today and in a week's time be less sure about it. This can happen to anyone. What do you say to the contradiction that Mr. Seselj has highlighted? This doesn't mean that you're a false witness and that you are lying. There is a contradiction here, and I'm sure you have an explanation for it. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this statement and the military authorities, in an article that I wrote in Sarajevo, I never had the opportunity of reading. As far as this statement is concerned, I had 15 minutes' time. I was given 15 minutes to sign all the pages, because all I wanted was to go home to see my mother, my sister, my brother, and not to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the explanation you provide is as part of the investigation, the investigator typed up this statement, and you signed it quickly, without reading it again? That is the explanation you give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2000, in the year 2000 -- or, rather, in 1999 or 2000, I'm not quite sure which, I asked to see -- to be shown this statement. This same man, Sacir Cedic, told me that I had voluntarily spent the time in detention and that I can't -- they wouldn't give the statement to me because it was given voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you understood something from what the witness just said, well, good luck to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. We'll get back to this point after the break. We must have a break now, and we're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the countdown is concerned, you have one hour left, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Koblar, we are going to look at the statements of the people who took you prisoner at Golo Brdo together. Could we please have document number 1 on the ELMO so that the witness could see the statement and the public as well, because this should be broadcast over the internet so that the public could see it. This is a statement of Miroslav Skoric, nicknamed Zuti, that's the man who was addressed as "Major" that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to put on the record that the OTP has received the statement about two hours ago, or maybe less, in Serbian, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ferrara, I notice, and this is something you're able to see also, that this was sent by Mr. Seselj's associates on the 11th of June at 11.54, which would explain why you received it two hours ago. Is that right, Mr. Seselj, number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the document that I received yesterday at two minutes past 2.00. It is the document marked with a Roman numeral I. I got it yesterday at two minutes past 2.00, and I had to read it first in order to decide whether I should use it or not. Last night, after finishing my work, I waited for one hour and fifteen minutes for transportation. So I could read the document only this morning, and it was then that I decided I would use it in cross-examination. Today, when I came to court, I gave it to the Registrar straight away so that it could be copied and distributed. So the speed was maximum, it couldn't have been any faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have it on the first screen. Have you put it properly? Oh, so that's what is not broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In these first paragraphs, so that we don't waste any time, please follow it, you have it in front of you, he says that he took part in the armed conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the very beginning, that his nickname is Zuti, and that he is well known by that nickname, and that Ilidza, Blazuj and Hadzici were fired at by the Muslims, as were other parts of Serb Sarajevo, and he talks about this big action of the Army of Republika Srpska. You see that in the statement, don't you? Then Miroslav Skoric, nicknamed Zuti, says of himself: "At the time, I was commander of the Intervention Company of the Tomo Veljancic Igman Brigade, military post code 7006." This unit that you called Brne's Chetniks, that was an informal name, whereas this is its formal name. Are you challenging that, do you doubt that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says that he commanded that unit, and he said that it was a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. And then he said: "There were no volunteers from elsewhere, from other republics or from Serbia, or volunteers of the Serb Radical Party." Was it your impression that some of those soldiers who had taken you prisoner were from elsewhere, not from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pajkovic, himself, is not from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Pajkovic is from Berane, like you, but he lived in Sarajevo. Pajkovic is from Berane, and that is why he treated you so badly, considering you to be a traitor, because the Bozovics are a famous Serb family in Berane and your mother is from the Bozovic. Your mother comes from the Bozovics; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She's Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about Pajkovic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Brne's unit, the only thing I knew was that Brne was from Sarajevo. And I recognised another man, who's name I'm not going to mention now, of course I won't, he still lives in Sarajevo and he just gave me an eye signal showing me that there was no chance of survival for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why didn't you want to mention his name?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he lives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does that have to do with anything? Is the situation there civilised?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they're civilised, but what about the situation for Bosniaks in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were always more civilised than in Sarajevo for Serbs. Didn't you kill 6.000 Serbs in Sarajevo during the war? It's in official documents.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you forgotten mathematics?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we cannot keep up with the speed of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you have to allow the interpreters to catch what you say, so please observe a small pause. You have been doing that very well until now, but I see that you get carried away sometimes. But try and respect the pause.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the questions have to come slower.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just go on praising the witness. I join you in praising the witness, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, no one is saying that we are complimenting the witness. This is in your mind. You are confounding him on a number of issues, which I think is extremely important, and I shall address this, because this cannot be set aside. Witness, this Zuti makes a statement. For Mr. Seselj, we will see what it contains. But in this statement, something technical is mentioned, something which he cannot have made up, the fact that his unit was number 7066. This can be checked on the VRS lists. This is something that can be checked. He can't have made this up, not something like that. If, in fact, his unit was an official VRS unit, why did you say that on the one hand, there was the VRS and, on the other hand, there was the Chetnik unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in addition to myself, three other men were taken prisoner. They are alive. Dragan Despotovic, who crossed over to the Army of Republika Srpska in camp; then Hasib Krslak and Hilmija Numic. They were taken prisoner by the military police of the Republika Srpska. They survived. As for myself and my three fellow combatants, we were taken prisoner by the Chetnik unit of Branislav Gavrilovic. I stated that clearly because, after all, I do make a distinction between Chetniks and Serbs. I never identified or did I allow other people to identify Serbs with Chetniks, Croats with Ustashas, or Muslims with balijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Seselj, on several occasions today, I don't know what the matter is, you call the Judges into question. You say that we are on the witness's side. We don't take anyone's side. The witness answers the questions, you put your questions, and we shall see, in the end, what we believe the witness is saying. This is how it works. Please stop accusing all the time. If you do not agree, file a request for impeachment. If you -- otherwise, just stop saying that we are taking sides. My colleague has put a question which is of a purely technical nature, and you turn around and say, "He's taking the witness's side." I don't understand. You have noticed that we put questions to the witness. We try to understand, with the help of the Prosecution, with the help of the witness, and with your help. We try to be completely neutral. We try to understand. The Prosecution has its case to present, you have your case to present. We shall see, in the end, where the truth lies. This is why there are legal proceedings like these. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do hope that you noticed the two substantive answers given by the witness. First of all, the witness did not manage to identify a single soldier in this unit that took him prisoner as a soldier outside -- from outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, except for this Pajkovic, who was born in Ivangrad. But my information says that he lived in Sarajevo, too, just like this witness was born in Ivangrad, called Berane beforehand, and now he lives in Sarajevo. That is one thing. Secondly, when I put to him the official name of the unit that was popularly known as "Brne's Chetniks," he said that that's not true, he said that that was a lie, whereas the official name of the unit was the Intervention Company of the Igman Brigade, Tomo Veljancic, military post code 7066. The OTP can check that out, and I think that the Trial Chamber has the right to instruct the OTP to check that out, and that will simplify matters. Here we are questioning witnesses without any kind of investigation taking place beforehand. We don't even have the autopsy findings of the three men who got killed at Golo Brdo, so all sorts of stories can be bandied about. We would know the cause of death had a proper postmortem been carried out. Now I'm going to continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I don't disagree on what you've just said, but I must say that if you feel that after what Mr. Zuti wrote to you, that his unit was part of the Company number 7066, which is a code name, what would have prevented you and your associates from sending a letter to the authorities to ask them officially that this be confirmed, i.e., that this unit was a member of the VRS at the time? Why haven't you done this? They would have responded by giving you a list, and you would have brought this list as evidence. I'm not saying that what you are saying needs to be dismissed. The best proof of it is that I put the question myself to the witness, to clearly emphasise it, and say, "Be careful, there might be a problem here," the problem which you raised yourself. The witness challenges this, but technically speaking you can say that this unit, first of all, was made up of people who were locals and not from Serbia, this is what you've said, and they were a part of the chain of command of the VRS. So that's it. There's no point in getting all worked up and getting irritated. All we're asking you to do is put questions of a technical nature and not be biased and think that the Judges are not listening to what you are saying. It's quite the opposite. We do listen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for years now the Army of Republika Srpska has not been in existence. Its entire documentation was transferred to Sarajevo. That is where the occupiers set up a unified Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we do not have any possibility of addressing the occupying forces or the forces that are under the control of the occupiers. Bosnia-Herzegovina is still a state under occupation. Formally, it is internationally recognised, but it is not an independent state. A Western governor is in power there, Lajcak.
