utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are right to say this. We know that the archives of the VRS have been transferred to Sarajevo. You are saying that Bosnia-Herzegovina is in a very specific legal situation. Fine, but why -- what prevents you from writing a letter to the High Representative if you believe that he's the competent person so that this person, you know, would intervene with local authorities in order to provide you with the lists? You can do this, you can write a letter. And if you run into any difficulties, then you can seize the Trial Chamber so that the Trial Chamber can step in. First thing. Second thing now, and you said it yourself. Bosnia-Herzegovina has an army at the moment, so why can't you just write to the Minister of Defence, asking him to have access to the archives? If he doesn't answer your letter, seize the Trial Chamber, and then we will request these documents to be disclosed to you. And they have to do it because of the cooperation agreements. This is the procedure that exists. You can do this. If for your defence, for cross-examination purposes, you run into problems, seize the Trial Chamber of these problems.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the basic problem of this trial, and many other trials before this Tribunal, is the fact that the OTP doesn't really carry out any investigations. All of this was supposed to be done in the investigation stage, so if an assertion is made that three soldiers of the Muslim army were killed, then all the postmortem findings should be brought here. Secondly, I would rather die than write a letter to Lajcak. I'm certainly not going to do that. But a few years ago, I asked the Trial Chamber, and you were a member, I asked that documents be provided to me under subpoena, all the documents pertaining to my name from the archives of the secret police, military and civilian, from the Federation, and from Croatia, America, England, France and Germany. And the Trial Chamber denied me that, and that is a fait accompli, as far as I'm concerned. So now I'm continuing my work in the knowledge that I will never receive this material. Of course, had I received this material, I would have had a lot more documents, whereas this way I am compelled to look for eyewitnesses. I was not on the spot. I had to find people who were on the spot. I had to find the people who took this man prisoner, this witness, and to hear their side of the story, and that is what I'm using now. I cannot humiliate myself and ask the enemy of the Serbian people for help in the proceedings that are instituted against me, and I'm not going to do that. So, please, let me continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, continue. At least I gave you my answer, as far as procedure is concerned. I told you that you have the possibility of seizing the Trial Chamber. You don't want to do this. You told us why. Everything is on the transcript. I'm not going to comment on this. But you know that in terms of the procedure, you have the possibility of seizing the Trial Chamber. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Again we are going to skip this part where Mr. Skoric explains how this unit, as an elite unit, was used to break through enemy lines and take strategic positions, and so on and so forth. Then he describes this attack against Golo Brdo, and he says: "The order for this operation was given to me by Colonel Spasoje Cojic, the staff of the Igman Brigade. The following units took part with us: The Intervention Platoon of the Igman Brigade; the Armoured Mechanised Company of the Ilidza Brigade, better known as the Serb Guard, Ilidza; the Reconnaissance/Sabotage Platoon Munja of the Igman Brigade. Have you heard of the names of these units?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard of the unit of the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Only of the Igman Brigade, as such?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you doubt that Mr. Skoric was in the Intervention Company, Tomo Veljancic, of the Igman Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the BH Army, we also have about 50.000 people who are registered as belonging to the BH Army from Day 1, and in actual fact they were outside, out of Bosnia, or in basements, or who knows where. If this is Plavi, he could have been registered I don't know where, but, I mean, he couldn't have been a member of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did you never mention in your statements to the Muslim -- don't interrupt me. If the Judges are not going to warn you, I'm going to warn you persistently. You are not supposed to interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we cannot interpret this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj does not need to intervene. I already told you that as far as procedure is concerned, you are here to answer the questions put to you by the accused. The procedure is very different from the procedure that exists in your country. The legal proceedings are different in your country, but here the accused is asking the question and you're supposed to just answer his questions, and nothing else. This is, of course, under the control of the Trial Chamber, because we want to make sure that no time is wasted and that the questions are relevant. And he's also supposed to ask you questions that are not offensive. This is the only control we have. Otherwise, he's entitled to ask all questions he wishes. And your right is to answer the questions, even if you don't agree with them, even if you're not happy with them, if you feel hurt. The question was put to you, and you must absolutely answer the question, either by "yes," "no," "I don't agree," "You're right," "You're wrong." That's the rules of the game here. The people who invented these rules of procedure decided that it would work this way. There was another possibility, which was to allow the Judges to have a major role, but that was not chosen, so this is the rules of the game. Defence is asking questions to you. You're supposed to answer these questions, even if you don't like them. These are the rules that were designed, and we have to play by the rules. So, Mr. Seselj, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Answer my question. Why, in neither of these two statements to Muslim military authorities, did you mention that the soldiers who captured you had signs with skulls and bones? Why isn't it in any of these two statements?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's not. Let the Prosecution help you and find it. It's not there. One statement is more than 30 pages long, the other one is 9. This is not there. The Prosecution can use its technology to find that very quickly, whether there is any reference to skull and bones. You claim, if I understand you correctly, that you mentioned these signs with skulls and bones, and you claim it's in the statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're not that sure anymore?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be there. I will repeat what I said a moment ago. I know what should be in the statement, but I had no occasion, neither with the Prosecution or the investigative authorities of my unit, to reread it before signing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So let's see how Zuti describes this action on Mount Igman. He gives a brief overview of your whole story about your capture at Mount Igman. This is the other side of the story: "The action on Mount Igman began with artillery preparation, and I --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I don't want to cut you off, but you asked a question earlier that's extremely important and I wish to come back to it. Mr. Seselj justly noted that in your statement, a 1994 statement made to the authorities of your country, and when you escaped and came back, you did not mention the skull-and-bones insignia. This is quite surprising. Why is that? The investigators who met with you and tried to find out what happened, you know, any investigator must absolutely ask the victim, and you were the victim in this case, whether he had any elements to identify the perpetrators. And when you carry out this kind of investigation, you have to ask the victim how the perpetrators were dressed, what kind of weapons they had, whether they had emblems, insignia, patches, and so on. These were the questions that they were supposed to ask, and apparently these questions were not asked. Now, was it because they were so convinced that these were soldiers from Republika Srpska and not from a Chetnik unit that there was no doubt about this, because that could explain why no questions were put to you on identification, or maybe they were in a frame of mind and they just were not concerned at the time to know exactly who did what. Now, after that, you met with people from the OTP. In your statement of 2004, April 22nd and 23rd, there we have mention of the skull-and-bones emblem. When I saw this, I wondered. You know, I'm fully transparent, contrary to what Mr. Seselj believes, I'm neither for one side nor the other. I don't side with anyone. I just want to get to the truth. So when I saw this, I said to myself, why is it that suddenly, when the witness has his -- is bringing us his document for the Red Cross and his injuries and so on, why is it that we have this document suddenly? So this is my question to myself: Did the witness volunteer this to the OTP or is it the OTP who showed the emblem to the witness so that -- to ask him, "Did you see this," or, "You did see this emblem?" So please tell me. When the investigator, in 1994, put questions to you, did he mention this emblem to you? Did he address this problem of the skull and bones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was under investigation and in detention in my own unit, there was one, quote/unquote, "truth" that I was supposed to sign; namely, that the platoon of 20 Serbs betrayed Golo Brdo, and I mentioned that in the statement. But in that statement, there should also be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. This hadn't escaped me. I really wondered why was it that he is going to be detained by his own friends. That was one problem, and obviously no one thought about this. Maybe Mr. Seselj was going to address this, but up until now nobody had addressed this. You are detained because your own side believes that maybe people -- there were traitors, and you're suspected of having betrayed. And you're saying now that you believe that the investigation was very biased. Thank you, you're being very specific now. So their purpose was to find out whether there had been betrayals or not, rather than trying to find out who were the perpetrators of these crimes; is this what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly, or maybe in other words, but in the same sense, to maintain the truth that 20 Serbs betrayed Golo Brdo, and that was later covered in the press and it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes, but the Judges are here to understand. Otherwise, they wouldn't be Judges. The second thing: When you met with the OTP, people from the OTP, in 2004, tell us whether it is the OTP who showed you this emblem [indicates] on the photocopy that you signed, or did you volunteer this photocopy and bring it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I brought an article that ran in series that also carried some photographs. That's a liberty I gave to the editor of "Vecernje Novine" newspaper, to insert some photographs. And in that article there is one photo, I don't know where it comes from, depicting Chetniks carrying weapons, and the first time I saw these photos was perhaps a month ago, when I got into contact with the OTP to decide whether I should come here to testify or not. Nobody imposed it on me or showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good, very well. So you're saying that the skull and bones thing, this skull-and-bones insignia, is something you volunteered, and no one told you anything about it; you spoke about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about it from my memory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I hope that you, too, have before you this long statement of the witness, some 30 densely-typed pages. Perhaps it would be even 100 pages with different spacing. It must be translated into English. The Prosecution gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have it. Now, Mr. Seselj, once again, I think sometimes there are misunderstandings, because you don't know what we have on the Bench. Today, for this witness, the Prosecutor gave us a file with all the exhibits that were to be shown to the witness, and in this file there was the written statement of 2004. But as to the statement made to the Muslim authorities in 1994, which was disclosed to you, it was not disclosed to us. We don't have it on the Bench. This is how things stand. You know many things, because the Prosecutor sent many documents to you and disclosed them to you, and if you think that we have it, we know about it also, but we don't. The only thing we have is what the Prosecution gave us, and the Prosecutor did not give us the 1994 statement. I just don't have it. So I believe that this is why we have such misunderstandings. I'm trying to give you as much information as I can. I'm telling you exactly what we do, what problems we run into, what questions we would like to ask. We are fully transparent here on the Bench. You raised your hand. What did you want to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to draw your attention, Mr. President, that you are taking over the terminology of the accused, referring to Muslim authorities. This is a statement or statements that I gave to legal investigative authorities of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, I agree with you. I fully agree with you, but we mention Muslim authorities because at the time when you escaped, you escaped from Kula and went back to the 101st Motorised Brigade. It's not a Serbian unit; it's a Muslim unit. We have three components; Croat units, Muslim units and Serbian units. This is how you must interpret the way we use "Muslim." On the field, there are three sides, Croats, Serbs or Muslims, which is why I use this terminology. Mr. Seselj, please resume. I apologise for having cut you off, but I wanted to really address the skull-and-bones insignia problem, because I believed it was very important. I wanted to get to the bottom of this and understand what really happened, but resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In this long statement on 34 densely-typed pages, that's about 100 pages of journalistic typing, you describe in detail all the soldiers who captured you, and the emblems they wore, and you mentioned cockades with two-headed eagles. Why didn't you mention the skull and bones anywhere? The Prosecution had time to check it. They didn't find it, either, and now we see it's not there. I have no time to read it all to you here, but it is absolutely not there. You did not mention that any of these soldiers had the skull-and-bones sign. Why?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that statement, there has to be even the name, the Chetnik unit of Brne Gavrilovic, Pla ve, Copo and Pajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's not Plave, it's blue. It's Zuti, yellow. A man with blonde hair is Zuti.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say. He was referred to as "Major," actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is there that it was the Chetnik unit, but there is no reference to skull-and-bones emblem. There is no dispute that they were called Chetniks and they called themselves Chetniks. That's not in dispute, but there is no reference to the skull and bones.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not my problem. If it's the Chetnik unit of Brne Gavrilovic, if Copo, Pajkovic and Major are mentioned, there should be also a detailed description - you say there is - of these people, plus the other one whom I didn't name here. It has to be there in the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution had more than half an hour to find the reference to skull and bones. I can only note they didn't find it. I really cannot dwell on this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: There is no reference to skull and bones, and there is no reference to cockade with two eagles, as the accused says. So there is no reference to any kind of insignia in this statement, so the accused is misunderstanding the statement of the -- it's on line -- page 59, line 1 and 2. He didn't describe any kind of insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, I don't really understand. Mr. Seselj says based on the 1994 statement, that the witness mentioned cockades and gave details. And in the document which I don't have, unfortunately, but which you must have and which must have been translated into English, I hope, you say that there is no mention -- Mr. Seselj said that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj says that there's no mention of the skull and bones there. This is what he's saying, anyway, but you have the document, so you can check. I can't check because I don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Seselj said a different thing. He said the witness described soldiers with cockade, two eagles, so soldiers that were not SRS member of Chetniks unit. It did not describe people with skull and bones. The truth is that the witness didn't describe any kind of insignia in the statement. There is no description of eagles, of an insignia, badge, skull or bones. There's nothing to do with the description of their uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since we established there is no reference to skulls anywhere, I will look for the cockades later. I'm really not interested in that now. It's important that the Prosecutor confirmed there is no reference to skull and bones, which was the point the witness made in examination-in-chief. I started to summarise for you the description of the situation given by Miroslav Skoric, nicknamed Zuti, in the course of the action on Mount Igman. He says: "The operation on Igman started with artillery preparation ..." That's where you agree: "... and I led my unit in an attack against fortified enemy positions on Golo Brdo elevation. Some 200 metres away from enemy bunkers, we were waiting for the artillery preparation to finish. In order to approach as unobserved as possible, I selected four soldiers, whom I led, to capture the bunker. I decided on this tactic after reconnoitering the terrain, when I noticed that everything was mined with directional fragmentation mines." You noticed that as well, these mines: "When we got to the bunker, we saw three dead enemy soldiers." That's what Zuti says: "We saw some more dead in the trench that was part of the bunker. Since the bunker was closed, we didn't know if there was anyone inside." In your opinion, is this a truthful description given by Zuti, who captured you at Golo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that the Major had captured me, but Pajkovic. And in this statement from the other side of Igman, from the side that they had come, because they came from the direction of Ilidza, they could see -- they could see, because on Golo Brdo there were just two directional fragmentation mines, and they could not see any dead soldiers, because they had captured them and they were alive when Pajkovic brought me. All three of them were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now turn to the second page, please, and we'll go through the statement further on. Zuti goes on to say: "After my call to surrender, from the bunker a rifle was thrown up." That's the bunker where you were: "And immediately afterwards, a man came out, and I asked him whether there was anyone else in the bunker. He said that he was alone and that his name was Perica Koblar. He added that he was a Croat by ethnicity, although nobody asked him that." Is it true that you declared yourself as a Croat?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. And let me repeat, I was not captured by the Major but by Pajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. The Major says he captured you. And did you ever declare yourself as a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he got a medal for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever declare yourself as being a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was that? When did you declare yourself as being a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in 1997, when I was at the elections, and I didn't declare myself; it was other people who wrote that in, who made that entry, and said that my ethnicity was Slovenian. I was at the independent candidate selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they put that entry there against your will, against asking you your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you never publicly declared yourself a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 2000, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in 1996, you did not?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why I would do that in 1996. The only document that you can obtain from 1996 or that you could find in 1996 was the OSCE document, when I was head at the electoral staff of the late Vladimir Srebrov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I haven't got any documents. I'm just leafing through some papers. All I'm interested in is: When was it that you declared yourself a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or was that in 1996? That was the first year after --

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a fax earlier on, and could this be shown to the witness. It is a report from the Founding Assembly of the Inmates Association of Bosnia-Herzegovina, camp inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember the founding meeting of the detainees of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since you're that informed, do you know what happened before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was a big scandal. A Muslim evinced hatred to everybody who was not a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then it should become clear to you, why I declared myself a Slovene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have just told us that you have received a document. Maybe you got it during the break. In that case, the Prosecution has not been made aware of it. You should and must disclose to the Prosecution any document you're going to be using. Mr. Ferrara, you didn't get this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I use this just by chance now, because the witness claimed that he did not declare himself in 1996 as a Slovene, and here on page 2, if you turn it over to page 2 -- I'm not interested in the document at all. This woman doesn't seem to understand me either. [In English] Turn on the second page in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's also on the web page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I have to speak that odious language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see here, your statement is being quoted, where you say: "First of all, I'm a Slovene, a Catholic, but that did not prevent me ...," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. One always has to be wide awake in your presence, because you say so many things. You just said -- you just mentioned this awful language. Which language are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English. The usher doesn't understand me, and to save time I had to speak up in that horrible language. What can I do? I didn't want to do that. It just escaped me, Mr. President, and I withdraw everything I said in that hateful language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not go into a discussion on language. Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At that Assembly, did you declare yourself, publicly, that you were a Slovene and a Catholic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Catholic, yes; a Slovene, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So is what it says on this web page not true?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not where it says that I'm a Slovene, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Return the document. I'm not interested in what you are at all.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because you said didn't declare yourself that way in 1996, where we see that you did, in fact?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're playing around you, playing around with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Listen, you're such a useful witness as far as I'm concerned that even if I'd wanted to invent you as a witness, I couldn't have done a better job. You've been god-sent here and serve my purpose perfectly. But let's go back to page 2 of the statement of Mr. Miroslav Skoric. He goes on to say they took you back to hand you over to the military police, and now he describes an interesting moment, an interesting detail. He says -- have you put the document back to page 2, page 2 on the ELMO? Is it on the ELMO? He says: "My unit left the positions taken control of and it was replaced by units from the other echelon, whose sole task was to take control and retain the positions gained. Within the composition of those units were people from Blazuj, and they were exposed to sniper fire from Golo Brdo. In order to avoid possible problems in escorting the prisoners, we put a flak-jacket on him." Is that true, that they put a flak-jacket on you so that when the other soldiers went down from Igman with you, you wouldn't be threatened, your life wouldn't be threatened?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you use the singular or the plural?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I am asking you whether the Serb soldiers who had captured you put on a flak-jacket to -- for your safety.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you said "prisoners," you used the word "prisoners" in the plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I am using the second-person plural as an individual, as -- that's a mark of my good behaviour. I said: Did they place a flak-jacket on you? I didn't say "flak-jackets," as relating to more people. I said "flak-jacket" in the singular, so don't waste my time.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brne did that, the Major did that, Copo did that and Pajkovic. The flak-jacket, a transportation sack, a military sack - I don't know what it's called - and I had to carry an M-84 or the sower of death, as we used to call it in Sarajevo, over my left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that I could -- you could resemble a Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, wearing a black shirt and black trousers, could I have resembled a Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you could have appeared like a Serb soldier because they gave you a flak-jacket and a powerful weapon. There were other Serb soldiers who did not have the proper uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down, and could the witness repeat his answer? It's too quick to translate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. Did they provide you with a flak-jacket to torment you or to protect you or, rather, to camouflage you if you came across somebody who wanted to take revenge on you? So were you given a flak-jacket to wear and heavy weapons to torment you or to save you? Just answer me that.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To carry as a mule.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you served for carrying a machine-gun and a flak-jacket, so that was a form of torture, was it? Say that, then. So they tortured you by giving you a flak-jacket, whereas they say they gave you a flak-jacket to wear to protect you. You say it was torture. All right, fine. The Dutch police provide me with a flak-jacket here. They say they're protecting me. I consider that they are torturing me with that flak-jacket, but that's a matter of personal opinion. Anyway, you got the flak-jacket before you met Branislav Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You say it's not, then it's not. It says here -- Zuti says that Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, at that time was being treated from the serious wounding in his abdomen and spine, and he found it difficult to move. So in the company, he dealt with the training of new soldiers. Did you ever notice that Branislav Gavrilovic was a man who had been seriously wounded? By the way he moved and walked, his behaviour, did he give the impression of somebody who had been seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday and I'll repeat that again today. When he was introduced, the Major introduced him, and he said, "This is Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, a Chetnik vojvoda of Vojislav Seselj's, for whom we thought, we, the BH Army, thought that he was dead, was left lying dead at Zeljo Stadium."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where you surrounded his volunteer unit at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about November 1993, when an attack was launched on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the attack on what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That wasn't the attack on Grbavica; it was April/May 1992; is that right? They were different battles?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. You thought he was dead. Well, luckily, he survived. And, finally, not to spend too much time on Miroslav Skoric's statement, he goes on to say the following: "After the war, I heard and read quite a different version of the events linked to Golo Brdo as presented by Perica Koblar. I was unpleasantly surprised, especially as the enemy side also knows that in addition to Koblar, in previous actions and later actions I behaved in a soldierly fashion towards all the prisoners, seven or eight of them, which was the total number. They are alive and well. In conformity with military procedure, they reached their homes." And at the end of the statement, he says that he agrees that I use his statement in the Court and that he was ready to be a witness of mine.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Major can come in, you can face him here in person. Brne is the only man who can claim something, who can state something, whereas everything that the Major states in that statement, the flak-jacket was put on me after Krajisnik had been killed and Rusmir had been killed, and then Brne took me away to the military police. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday, when you answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution, I was very surprised by them, in terms of their logic. Sometimes in life, there are irrational things that happen, but if you address it from a purely logical standpoint, some people were captured and a number were executed. Strangely enough, you were not executed, so this raises a question: Why was he not executed like the others? Out of the four, three died, and the fourth miraculously spared. Why is that the case? This is what a reasonable judge may well ask. After that, we find out, this is something you've said already, that this group will protect you, since when you were taken to the premises of the military police, Gavrilovic says to the others that you should not be mistreated and so on and so forth, even though you were mistreated. This is what you said. And then something else crops up. Zuti, I don't know if what he -- if he's telling the truth or not, but whatever the case may be, this flak-jacket is mentioned, and you confirmed this. You say "yes." So I don't understand anymore. You were one of the four men that were captured in the bunkers, and strangely enough, you are spared. And after that, you are given a flak-jacket to protect you from whom? Who can shoot at you, since you have just said that there were no Muslim units on the spot? So why were you given a flak-jacket? I find this difficult to comprehend. I'm sure you are going to shed some light on this, but how is it? Of course, when the police arrests an individual, this individual is being protected and given a flak-jacket because one is afraid that some people might want to take a shot at him. This is a well-known technique. At the time, who could have made attempts at your life, since three were killed by members of the group and it's that same group which kills those three men who, strangely enough, are going to protect you by giving you a flak-jacket? I don't understand. Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me repeat. At Golo Brdo, one co-fighter of mine was killed straight away. Down there in front of Brne, two others were killed. I was spared because I brandished a pistol, whereas the flak-jacket and all the rest of it wasn't given to me to protect me, but so that they could see how much I could take. Who would they be protecting me from? There were no snipers over there, because that's the area of Mount Igman and the BH Army -- not the BH Army, but the de-miners started arriving in the region after the reintegration of the Sarajevo municipalities, only after that. And what the accused is trying to emphasise, that's obviously a way of making little of the witness and the Court, to put a flak-jacket on to torture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's another question. You are saying that you were a given a flak-jacket to test you, to see how much time you could wear it. I don't know. I have worn a flak-jacket, like many people, in special circumstances, but it doesn't weigh 100 kilos or 50 kilos. It's bearable by any standards, so I don't understand. If they wanted to test you, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat again. In the context of what it says, I didn't say that somebody tortured me. I said that it was put on me to see how much I could take, not for Brne, or Copo, or I don't know who else, the Major, to torture me, because that white Golf car -- well, we stopped off and had a break, to have a cigarette, and then we continued on our journey to the military police. Now, what the gentleman, the accused, is trying to highlight this torture business, I assume you're torturing him here in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If what you're saying is true, namely, that when you were captured the group killed four people --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Three people, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I find it difficult to understand how the fourth is spared, for what reason. Why is he given cigarettes? I think you even said that you were given coffee and you are being pampered, you are being given a flak-jacket. I don't understand. Why did they do all this just for you, why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this was interpreted to you yesterday, when I was saying that Brne kicked Zivko Krajisnik twice, and after that, with his fingers, he hurt his nostrils, and after that he gave him a pistol to kill the Ustasha, as he said. And when he didn't do it, then he gave me the pistol, and I took the pistol. And that very same second, Brne took the pistol and ordered the execution. In other words, it's not that I'm trying to portray myself here as a super hero or this or that. Quite simply, the man, and I'm talking about Brne --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here again, this is not understandable. You are being asked to kill your comrade. You are being given the pistol. Logically, he would have just waited for you to pull the trigger, but you say, strangely enough, he picked up the pistol instantly. That's not very logical, either. Why? Because he was afraid that you might shoot at him and shoot him. Maybe he was right, maybe you were going to shoot him. We don't understand. He gives you the pistol, asks you to shoot, and then in a split second takes the pistol away again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same pistol was first in Zivko Krajisnik's hands. At one moment, I nodded to Zika, in order to avoid Pajkovic's knife, and Brne noticed that, I guess, then he took the pistol and proffered it to me. I pointed it at Krajisnik, Brne took the pistol from me because if we were to apply logic to this, if you were to give a prisoner of war a loaded pistol, then he'd use it. I would use it against myself, if nothing else. That is what the police of Republika Srpska knows, the Major knows, Pajkovic knows, Copo knows, as mentioned by the accused, and he said that I was the only one that Brne got off his knife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You should know, since you did your military service, and I see that you even got a degree in Political Science from the university, that everyone who took part in this war knew full well that according to the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, it was strictly prohibited to kill civilians and to kill prisoners of war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I can hold against Brne is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that an answer to my question? I am asking you whether you know that everyone had to know that the Criminal Code strictly prohibited the killing of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So Brne had to know that, like all the other men from his unit, that the law strictly prohibited this; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Domazet taught you something, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, what kind of an answer is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is Dusan Domazet? I don't know who this person is. The question Mr. Seselj has put to you is this: Whether according to the Criminal Code in force, they could try war criminals; do we agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your view, Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, Miroslav Skoric, Zuti, and all the other members of this Intervention Company of Tomo Veljancic, knew that it was a crime to kill a prisoner of war; did they know that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you asking me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what do you think about that? Were they aware of the fact that this was a crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's putting a question to you. If prisoners of war are killed, this means there can be a penalty; is this right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, however the accused asks me whether Brne, Major, Copo and Pajkovic knew that. How could I know what four other men knew or thought?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say, then, that you can't answer the question. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did all the people in your army know that it was prohibited to kill prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Is it then a sound proposition that if all the Muslims in the army knew that it was prohibited to know -- that it was forbidden to kill prisoners of war, that all Muslims and all Croats knew that as well?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deal in suppositions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If your story were true, namely, that Brne's men really killed three prisoners of war after they were taken prisoner, and now they have a fourth one, how crazy should a man be if he already committed a serious crime that even carries the death sentence, according to Yugoslav law, to leave the only witness alive, give him safe passage to the military police, and then visit him for another six days in prison and bring him cigarettes and other gifts? Look, any criminal who'd kill three men would kill a fourth one so as not to leave an eyewitness behind. Now, explain this. Why did they kill three prisoners and then they left you alive so that you could testify about the crime some day? What's the logic in that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask Brne, because Brne is the one who sent me greetings during 1997 and 1998, during the election campaigns, from one of your presidents from the Dobrinja municipality. I mean, president of one of the municipal committees of the Serb Radical Party who saw Brne and who sent me greetings in Sarajevo through this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what does this have to do with anything? Did he consider you to be a friend? Is that why he sends greetings?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ask Brne.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Brne gave me a statement, too, and I left it as the fourth one for today. So I have Brne's statement about this same event, except that I left it for the end as a real treat. So if you don't eat up too much of my time, I hope that we get to this treat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, for your information, you have approximately 30 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you plan a break, Mr. President, because it's already 6.00 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. We might not have to have a break. One or two breaks. One, it's so riveting that I forget about the breaks, and the interpreters need breaks. I've been here since 6.00 in the morning, and I can go on through the night. We shall now have a 15-minute break and resume at a quarter past 6.00, because we have to finish with this witness today. We shall resume again at a quarter to [as interpreted] 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I believe that you have 30 minutes left, not a minute more. This is what the Registrar just told me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, that we finish before 7.00, but you know that that doesn't depend on me only. Could we please see on the ELMO this document number II, Roman numeral II.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know who Rajko Golijanin is; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surname is familiar, the name not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He states here that he knows you well. He gave you a statement -- he gave me a statement that arrived yesterday, and he describes there -- let's try to move through this statement faster, if you don't mind, and all of this in order to finish today so you don't have to come back tomorrow. Now, you deal with that. He describes here when he was mobilised in the Army of Republika Srpska, that he was trained for reconnaissance, and then he says in the second paragraph, during the fight for Golo Brdo, he was at the communications centre, the barracks in Blazuj. He also says that Branislav Gavrilovic at that time was in very poor health, and he asked him to drive him and to help him on that day. Do you remember the driver who drove Brne to you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because Brne was perfectly healthy. The way he kicked Zivko Krajisnik twice so forcefully, an ill man, a wounded man, could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Do you know who drove Brne to you when you were being taken down Igman?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Golijanin tells us here that Brne was mostly interested in what was going on with his co-fighters from the unit under the command of Zuti, and he told him to drive him to the road, "to the road that our fighters are going to reach when they come down from Igman," because he wanted to greet them. Now could you please show the third paragraph on the ELMO. Now, Golijanin says: "The fighters were arriving but I realised that they were bringing a person who had a flak-jacket and was not carrying a weapon. This caught my attention, and then I realised that it was an enemy prisoner of war. I didn't understand then why he wore a flak-jacket, but when I looked at him, he seemed familiar. I remembered he was a waiter from a Sarajevo cafe, but I didn't remember which one. Only later, I realised that Miroslav Skoric, Zuti, had taken off his own flak-jacket or taken another soldier's and that he gave it to the prisoner in order to keep him safe." That is what he says, and you don't remember this man, that he was in Brne -- with Brne when you got down there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 4, he says: "Since all the soldiers from the unit that was commanded by Miroslav Skoric, Zuti, gathered together, he decided that we transfer the enemy soldier to the barracks in Blazuj. In the car with me were Miroslav Skoric, Zuti, Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, and the enemy prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot keep up with this pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you claim that Brne was driving, and this man states that he was driving and that Zuti, Brne and you were in the car?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brne was driving. It's a Golf, with two cars [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slow down, both of you, slow down. The interpreters are having a hard time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is why this statement is interesting. He describes that he took you to the barracks in Blazuj, that Zuti handed you over to the officer in charge, and that he, Golijanin, took Brne to Ilidza, and then he says, and this is important, this is particularly important in his statement, the last paragraph on the first page and then we are going to turn to the second page: "I saw Perica Koblar another time after the war. That happened in 1996, at the time of the first elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the war. As a representative of the Serb Renewal Movement, I took a helicopter that belonged to the international forces from Sarajevo to Banja Luka, where there was a political meeting that was organised by the OSCE. Perica Koblar was in the same helicopter, who had set out to the same meeting in the capacity of an independent candidate for the Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you remember this helicopter flight to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1996, I flew to Banja Luka as head of the Election Staff of Vladimir Srebrov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Possibly, but do you remember the helicopter flight? Did you take this helicopter?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that Golijanin was in the same helicopter with you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. He remembers you and he says that you were in the same helicopter. I would not have known of this helicopter had Golijanin not written to me about this. We haven't mentioned the helicopter here yet. All right. Now, this is what Golijanin says: "Since Koblar's statements to Sarajevo newspapers that I read do not correspond to the truth at all, and I am an eyewitness to that truth, I asked him why he gave the journalist that response. He answered me, 'It had to be that way. What can you do?' The following persons were also in the helicopter, and they can confirm these words: Mirnes Ajanovic, president of the BOS party, and his vice-president whose name I do not remember, as well as Fadil Hadzic, president of the Workers Party, as well as a few representatives of other parties." Do you remember this conversation with Golijanin on the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the conversation. The only conversation I remember, and I don't remember the last name, was the one with Todor, who was president of the Municipal Committee of the Serbian Radical Party in Sarajevo. I don't remember Golijanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that helicopter, there were usually at least 15 of us, the representatives of all political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know this Mirnes Ajanovic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he with you in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Fadil Hadzic, president of the Workers Party?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall Fadil.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Rajko Golijanin claims that; that you were in the same helicopter, that you talked about it, and that that is the explanation you gave him. It had to be that way. What can I say?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, and in 1996 I did not give any statements to any newspaper in Sarajevo in relation to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You made statements already in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1994 -- yes, in 1994, a statement was recorded about the escape, and that is the only thing that is there, and then also what was published by a Catholic weekly. There was a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was on TV and in the Catholic weekly. See? So Rajko Golijanin is very well informed. Tell me, so you were in Serb imprisonment for seven months?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 17th of July, 1993, to the 17th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that seven months? Was my math right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was any Muslim prisoner in prison for more time than you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for those that I found there, it is certain that at least 70 stayed on after I left --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who were there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I found at Kula and who were there after I escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslim authorities didn't want to exchange you at all, although the Serbs were offering you for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladimir Srebrov and I both had our suspicions that this was a political question, namely, that the Serbs would not release us, because allegedly later on after the escape, it was said whenever Vladimir Srebrov and I were requested, and these exchanges, the Serb authorities asked for 50 or 100 Serbs from Sarajevo respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you never escaped from Kula, but the Serb authorities let you stroll over to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you realise how -- how senseless this question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think that what is far more senseless is that they should keep you there in prison for a long time and nobody expressed any interest in you, and nobody needed you, and why would the Serbs keep you in prison forever and the Muslims didn't want to exchange you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, why would they bring me to the Muslim positions if they knew that they would kill me? I'd have to explain who I was and what I had done with all the messages of the International Red Cross. Probably somebody would have broken my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You weren't sent to the Muslim positions, you were sent to UNPROFOR positions, to the positions of the UN forces, and then the UN forces took you in and handed you over to the Muslim authorities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. General Smith was at the airport then, and then the Serbs, after my escape, asked General Smith -- allegedly, they said that I was a Serb soldier who got lost and reached the airport, and then my messages sent to the Red Cross saved me from having UNPROFOR return me to Kula. And they contacted the International Committee of the Red Cross to check my identification number, the one that you saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What I have here is your birth certificate, too, and your mother's certificate. I have found everything about you.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You obviously have everything, but still there's still something lacking, as far as you're concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't be rude. Behave yourself here. You know, you cannot make statements like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, no comments, please. Refrain from comments. Let the accused put questions to you. Refrain from comments. It's useless. When Mr. Seselj makes comments, we also tell him to refrain from it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are giving him a lot of latitude in harassing witnesses and victims and turning them into guilty parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the cross-examination procedure is such that the accused is entitled to check your credibility. This is what the procedure allows. He can ask you very embarrassing questions. This is provided for in this procedure, and we have to live with it. He's not insulting you. As long as he's not attacking the honour of your family and so on, he can ask all the questions he wants. He can ask questions to you as to how you escaped. He can put questions to you regarding the ensuing detention after that to try and prove his case. He's entitled to it. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then when the United Nations turned you over to Muslim authorities, you were so suspect that the Muslim military authorities arrested you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not arrest me. That's one. And, two, concerning my escape, you already saw an official document from the International Red Cross. You saw the official document of the state commission, and you can check, because you have so many connections. You can also check with Skiljevic, who was then director of the Kula Prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not interested in those things. I'm interested -- to whom did the UN forces turn you over?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my personal request, because General Smith insisted that I must wait for the morning and that in the morning I go to a third country by plane, with mediation of the International Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I really don't want to know about this. Tell me, briefly, to whom did the UN forces turn you over? What Rupert Smith told you, I don't want to know.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To whom, your unit, 101 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to the Dobrinja Brigade that was close to the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who took you in there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security officer on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And where did they put you up?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I called my mother on the phone, and then they locked me up in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They locked you up in the basement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were not arrested?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they shut me there, and nothing was said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, usually when somebody is locked up in the basement, it's a form of arrest. If you don't want to call it arrest, let's say that they deprived you of liberty as they locked you up in the basement.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want to use legal terminology they deprived me of liberty for that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, deprivation of liberty, in legalese is called arrest. And after that night, where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, men from my unit came, but prior to that I showed Ismet Hadzic where the Serb positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And where did they take you then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And where did they put you up then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room where the police was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how much time did they spend talking to you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. You have that statement. I think there is a date on that statement, when it was completed, when the investigation was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you how much time you spent in the interview with the investigative authorities, the military police of the 101 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You escaped on the 7th of February; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For 12 days, you were locked up, plus that 1 day in that unit from Nedzarici -- where did you say they were from?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay, Dobrinja Brigade. That's 21 days. From the 7th of February, if you add 21 days, that's 10th of March. Did I do the sums right? That was not a leap year. So on the 10th of March, the interviews with you were completed, and the statement is dated 19th February, so it was ante-dated?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which statement do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The one you gave to the Muslim military authorities, the one we showed here.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I don't know what the date on that statement is, but at least 15 or 20 days I spent writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, very well. I believe you now, unlike what you said earlier. Where were you accommodated while the interviews were going on?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By day, the first few days I was in those rooms with Sacir Cedic, and then I was taken over by two investigators. And by day I would be outside of the barracks and in the evenings I wrote my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which apartment?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where is that apartment?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building where you said you were as a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 27 July, 61?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not where I lived when I was a student.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said yesterday you lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's not a students' hostel, you know. So when the interviews were all over, you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So on that statement, there should be -- the date should be the 10th of March or thereabouts, but we see, on the first page of the statement, "19 February." On that day, 19 February, you gave the statement voluntarily and with your full mental capacity; is that correct? That's written on the first page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's not that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This other one in small lettering, this is 34 densely-typed pages, it couldn't be any denser. You signed that statement; that's your signature?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that the statement you wrote in hand and then they retyped it?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this statement, I suppose, took two days only to type; there are only -- there are 100 standard pages?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took me ten days to write. It was in agreement with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, then, does it say that on 19 February, you see it in the preamble, on the premises of the Service of Military Security of the 101st Motorised Brigade, you gave voluntarily and in your full mental capacity to the authorised officer, et cetera, when it was completed within 20 days?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something you should ask of the commander of the Security Service and the officer in charge in the 101st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Even that is a satisfactory answer. Now, explain, why are there two statements with different texts, but dated the same day, 19th February, 1994, and you signed both of them? One statement has a larger spacing. I can show it on the ELMO. You signed it. You signed every page and you signed at the end. And the other page is 34 densely-typed pages, also signed by you. The date on both of them is 19 February. Why were two statements made? I can't understand this.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This second statement was given to the Commission for Investigation of War Crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: End of February -- sorry, not end of February. Not before the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it doesn't say it was made on the 20th of March. It says it was made on the 19th of February. There's no such date in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I hope you noticed that I did not waste this time for nothing, although ten minutes are left. You see very mysterious things are happening, things that we did not know before. That's why I devoted some attention to that, concerning the statements given by this witness. Everything is so mysterious, it couldn't be any more mysterious. Since only ten minutes are left, I have here a statement by Mladen Popovic, who also --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of him? Is that Copo?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who is he, then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know Copo's name?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He gave a statement here. We can show it on the ELMO, although I don't want to spend time on it. I want to move on to Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne's statement, and finish with that. His statement is completely identical to Zuti's statement concerning the way you were captured and transferred to the military police. Do you want to see it?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't doubt that it's identical?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I doubt it? If it's identical to the Major's, it can't be -- what Major said that he found, three dead men, can't be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to the statement of Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne. I have two of his statements, but we can't go through both of them. You can put the first page on the ELMO. Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne. Number 4. [In English] First page. [Interpretation] He makes a distinction between the time when he was a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party and, on the other hand, when he joined the unit Tomo Veljancic at Ilidza. I don't suppose it's very interesting for you. We'll leave it aside. Let's move on to page 2. You see here the details of Branislav Gavrilovic, his career during the war, until the time he joined the unit Tomo Veljancic, and he says due to poor health, injuries to his spine and stomach, the command of the unit was taken over by Zuti. We see that on the second page. On the following page, number 3, paragraph number 2, he says: "In the unit, there were no volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. The unit was made up of the Serbs from that part of Sarajevo and those who had fled from the Muslim part of Sarajevo and became duty-bound to join the military." Then he speaks about the training in the Savo Derikonja Training Centre, and then he speaks about the operation at Mount Igman. Brne says he followed the operation from the communication centre of the Command of the brigade and that he was there with Mile Staka, assistant commander of the Igman Brigade. Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He goes on to describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes. It's not very clear, the situation with these statements of Gavrilovic. The accused disclosed to us two statements just during the last break. On the first page of this statement is a statement of the 11th of June, 2008, so it's today, faxed today at 1.54. The second page of this statement is another statement faxed yesterday, 10 June 2008 at 2.00. That was given on the 9th of June, as you can check at page 4 of the statement, and I received this sort of authentication or something on the 10th of June. Page 5 of the statement. So I don't understand how many statements we have, when they were given, when they were -- and also this first statement was -- sought authentication in a different date, also it's today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, can you explain this to us, these two statements?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... said that there are two statements. First I got the longer one that begins with the second page marked "2" in hand, and then I asked for an additional statement and I got it on one page, where Branislav Gavrilovic stated very clearly when he was a volunteer of the Serb Radical Party and when he moved on to Ilidza, because I noticed it was missing from his main statement, and that was the only reason. The larger statement arrived yesterday. This one -- the other one arrived today. I said that there were two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are two statements, one which is dated the 10th of June, which comprises several pages, and today's statement, which is only one page long. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We are on page 3 now. Towards the bottom of that page, Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, describes how he went out to meet his fellow combatants, to congratulate them on their victory, and he says that along the whole way he was coming across various soldiers of various units of the Army of Republika Srpska, and after a while Skoric and members of his unit showed up. "I noticed," he says, "that they were leading a prisoner wearing a flak-jacket." So you got that flak-jacket before you met with him? You got it already at Golo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says it's true. Brne is a greater man than I, and I believe everything he says.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's certainly a greater man than you, but this statement is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How tall are you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking, how tall are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You could be a little shorter than that. And he says: "When all the fighting men gathered together, Skoric ordered that they all return to base near Ilidza, and the fact that I came by car, I used to transport the prisoner to the barracks in Blazuj. Skoric turned over the prisoner to the military police in Blazuj, and I returned." So he confirms in his statement what his other fighting man said, so that's not true, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true, and I hope the Prosecution will call another two survivors who were there with me, who will confirm that Brne took me to that prison. He threatened Despotovic, he didn't hit anyone, but he said, "If I had arrested you, you would not have lived."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brne.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those three of my other fellows who were arrested by the military police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why did he leave you alive so that you can testify how his fellow combatants killed three of your men?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to ask Brne. I have to say that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said in examination-in-chief that I commanded that unit; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was captured by the unit of Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, and that he, himself, said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have a statement by Mr. Gavrilovic which is worth what it's worth, but he says that when he arrived, you were already a prisoner and you were wearing a flak-jacket. This is what he says. And after that, you were taken to the military police. This is his version. Maybe he's telling the truth, maybe he's lying; I don't know. This is what we have. Mr. Seselj is putting questions to you. You stand by your version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, and I wish to repeat again. The three other men are alive who saw Brne bring me to prison, to Blazuj, and he didn't mistreat those three men. He just said, "Had I captured you, you wouldn't be sitting there now." Those men are alive. I don't know about Dragan Despotovic, but the other two, my fellow combatants, are, thank goodness, alive and well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During examination-in-chief, you said Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, led a unit which was under my command. That's what you said in the examination-in-chief, and that must be in the transcript somewhere.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Chetnik unit of Branislav Gavrilovic, whose god, whose number-one man is Vojislav Seselj, and when he threatened Zivko Krajisnik, he said that not Mladic, not Karadzic, not Krajisnik could save him, because you are the be-all, end-all, the god in Sarajevo and the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, we in the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik Movement never mention God's name in vain. There are no gods among us, and I would be very proud if this unit of Brne's and that Intervention Company was under my platoon. That would make me very proud. Unfortunately, it was not.
